subject: system-design
title: Non-Functional Requirements Checklist
summary: The qualities to pin down before designing anything, because availability, consistency, latency, and scale pull a design in different directions.

blocks.text: Functional requirements say what a system does: post a tweet, place an order, send a message. Non-functional requirements (NFRs) say how well it has to do it: how fast, how reliable, at what scale. Two systems with identical features but different NFRs are designed completely differently, so you ask about the NFRs up front.
The checklist to ask up front

items: Availability: what uptime is required, and what happens during a failure?
Consistency: must every read see the latest write, or is slightly stale data fine?
Latency and throughput: what's the target response time, and how many requests per second?
Scalability: what's the expected scale today, and how fast will it grow?
Durability: can data ever be lost once written?
Security and privacy: who can access what, and what data is sensitive?

blocks.text: These aren't a formality. Each answer changes concrete choices. A strict latency target might force a cache or a CDN. A high-availability target pushes you toward replication and multiple regions. A durability target dictates how many copies of the data you keep and where.
The tensions you'll have to resolve

The interesting part is that NFRs conflict. Strong consistency and high availability pull in opposite directions during a network partition. You can favor one only by relaxing the other. Tight latency often means serving slightly stale, cached data; strict consistency often means a slower write path. There's no design that maxes out everything.

blocks.title: Name the tradeoff out loud
blocks.text: When two NFRs conflict, say which one you're prioritizing and why. 'This is a feed, so I'll favor availability and accept eventual consistency' shows you understand the tension rather than ignoring it.

Every later decision is an answer to an NFR: database choice, caching, partitioning, replication. If you skip this step, you're guessing at the targets, and a design built on guessed targets can't be evaluated. The checklist turns a vague prompt into a concrete spec you can design against.
Requirements drive every decision downstream, so pin them before you design. Five minutes of clarifying questions saves you from solving the wrong problem for the next forty.
